newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Albanian love affair with German luxury cars.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Albanian love affair with German luxury cars.

text.p: Prices in Albania's unusual second hand car market vary widely, depending on the answer to one key question -- Do you plan to drive only in Albania, or take the vehicle abroad?

It is a question asked by every self-respecting car dealer in the land, and customers content with driving within Albanian borders can pay as little as one-fifth of the price asked of those interested in foreign travel.

For Europe's poorest country is awash with stolen cars, especially Mercedes-Benz, the status symbols once driven only by the communist elite in a land where private car ownership was outlawed until 1991.
A nearly new Mercedes-Benz for home use only can cost as little as $6,000.

"There is a kind of gentleman's agreement between buyer and seller," said a 35-year-old car dealer named Avni. "If you want the car at a reasonable price, the buyer has to solve the problems with documents himself. If you want a car with documents, it will cost more."
There are an estimated 500,000 cars in Albania, up from about 5,000 six years ago, and about 60 percent of them are thought to be Mercedes.

Random surveys support that: on one main street in central Tirana, six of 11 cars at one traffic light were Mercedes; nine out of 20 at a parking lot were Mercedes. Everywhere you look, you will see them, often 1980s models, slightly battered but ruggedly traversing the pot-holed streets of Tirana, Durres and Vlore.
"Mercedes are the only cars that can survive these roads," said one Tirana driver. "The Germans make good cars. The French and Italian cars don't hold up as well."
THE MOST POPULAR CAR IN ALBANIA
President Sali Berisha once said there were more Mercedes per capita in Albania than anywhere else in the world.

At a 1996 election rally, he reminded voters that their dreams about prosperity were being fulfilled under his government. "You dreamed of having villas instead of bunkers...you dreamed of owning a car and now Albanians have the highest number of Mercedes per capita," Berisha said.
In the days of Stalinist dictator Enver Hoxha, who ruled for 40 years, only the elite could cruise past pedestrians and cyclists in luxurious western limousines -- usually Mercedes.
Most Albanians know that many of the Mercedes now crowding the streets are stolen. In some places, drivers don't even bother to remove the German licence plates and national stickers on the cars.

But in a country where the average monthly wage is $70, few seem unduly alarmed that western luxury cars can be had for as little as $1,000 -- provided you stay in Albania and avoid those embarrassing confiscations by other countries' border police.
"I would say at least 80 percent of the cars in Albania were stolen and then 'imported' from Germany, Italy and Bulgaria," said one dealer in Tirana.
One taxi driver named Ilir said he had paid some $11,000 for his year-old silver BMW, which he said he loved like a child.
"I don't care whether it is stolen," he said. "I was given ready-made papers and the guarantee I'll get half my money back if there are problems with the police later on."

But he admitted he was advised not to drive the car outside Albania, and especially not in Turkey, where the dealer said police regularly run computer checks on cars coming from Albania, Romania and Bulgaria.

A splendid red Porsche went on sale at half-price in the rebel-held town of Vlore last month, a clear sign of decline in the southern port, where most people's life savings went into pyramid investment schemes that collapsed earlier this year, triggering an armed uprising.
These days, cars are not always bought for cash. "An Opel, in good shape, is exchanged for 60 Kalashnikovs in the southern town of Gramsh," wrote the daily Dita Informacion.

Gezim Gjolena said he has sold more than 50 cars over the past three years, mostly Mercedes. His brother lives in Germany and sends him two or three cars a month, which he usually sells for between $3,000 and $6,000.

"We provide our clients with the necessary papers, so that they will have no problems with the Albanian police," he said, insisting that most cars were bought in Germany quite cheaply. But a colleague said about half of them had been stolen.
Avni, a middleman between dealers and buyers, said the cars are often stolen in Germany or Italy and documents somehow procured before the cars are transported to Albania.

Sometimes documents are forged, sometimes the owners make deals with the car thieves in insurance scams. And sometimes cars are bought with legitimate documents -- especially older models that may no longer pass inspection in Germany.
But dealers shrug their shoulders and say bribing police in Albania and en route is part of the cost of their business.
Avni said he can get documents fairly easily in Albania by bribing police here. He works closely with one officer who is trying to feed his family on a monthly salary of $65.
A German once spotted a picture of his stolen Mercedes while reading a magazine in Hamburg. He made frantic calls to the Albanian photographer to try to discover where he had seen the car.
Not all would-be owners know about the shady origins of their car.
Former central bank governor Ilir Hoti took over a Mercedes from his predecessor, but when he drove it to Italy several years ago, it was found to have been stolen.
Only after lengthy explanations was he allowed to keep it.
